lectures.title: Name the feature, then read its value
lectures.hook: A fictional clinic records resting heart rates of 64, 72 and 80 beats per minute. What stays the same across the three records, and what changes?
lectures.example_label: Synthetic teaching records; no real patient measurements. Expert content review pending.

scenario_image.alt_text: A clinician reviews anonymised heart-rate records while patients rest in a clinic; the illustration is context, not the example data.

worked_steps.title: Choose a feature
worked_steps.text: Resting heart rate is the feature recorded for each person. Its name tells us what to look for in every row.

worked_steps.title: Read a value
worked_steps.text: For one record, the value is 72 beats per minute. The number is a value of heart rate, not a different variable.

worked_steps.title: Compare records
worked_steps.text: Other records can have different values of the same feature. A variable need not change in every row; it needs to be capable of taking different values.

lectures.definition: A variable is a feature that can take different values. A value is a particular instance of that feature, such as one recorded heart rate.
lectures.pitfall: Do not confuse the variable's name with one person's value. A constant value in a small sample does not, by itself, make a feature incapable of varying.
lectures.takeaway: Ask: what feature are we recording, and what value does it have in this case?
lectures.challenge_title: Fresh case: a count in a dashboard

lectures.title: Notice a pattern across records
lectures.hook: Fictional records show that people reporting more weekly exercise also tend to have lower resting heart rates. What does the recorded pattern describe?
lectures.example_label: Synthetic teaching example; not an empirical exercise study. Expert content review pending.

scenario_image.alt_text: People gather after casual exercise while a researcher reviews anonymous records; the picture does not supply the association data.

worked_steps.title: Find two variables
worked_steps.text: The records contain reported exercise and resting heart rate. Each person contributes values for both features.

worked_steps.title: Describe how they vary
worked_steps.text: In this fictional dataset, higher exercise values occur alongside lower heart-rate values. Variables can be associated while moving in opposite directions.

worked_steps.title: Report the pattern carefully
worked_steps.text: Say which values tend to occur together across the records. One isolated heart-rate reading is not itself a pattern between the two variables.

lectures.definition: An observed association is a pattern in how variables occur together or vary together in the records.
lectures.pitfall: Association does not require both variables to increase. One can tend to decrease as the other increases.
lectures.takeaway: First describe the recorded relationship between the variables in plain language.

source_refs.locator: Section 1.1, pages 1-2, joint observations and distributions

lectures.challenge_title: Fresh case: a pattern in a product log

lectures.title: A shared pattern is not yet a cause
lectures.hook: A fictional city records that ice-cream sales and sunglasses sales rise together. Would stopping ice-cream sales change sunglasses sales?
lectures.example_label: Synthetic city example; proposed explanations are hypotheses. Expert content review pending.

scenario_image.alt_text: A sunny market has an ice-cream stall beside a sunglasses display; it illustrates the setting without establishing a causal direction.

worked_steps.title: Separate the observation
worked_steps.text: The records describe sales rising together. That is a statement about the observed pattern, not the result of an action on either shop.

worked_steps.title: Consider an alternative
worked_steps.text: Warm, sunny days could influence both purchases. This is a possible shared explanation; proposing it does not establish that it is the true explanation.

worked_steps.title: Ask the action question
worked_steps.text: Stopping ice-cream sales changes one part of the situation. The recorded association alone does not tell us whether sunglasses sales would change.

worked_graph.label: One possible explanation, not established by the sales records
worked_graph.note: This partial hypothetical graph shows a possible shared cause. It does not settle the effect of changing either kind of sale.

lectures.definition: Association describes how variables vary together. An observed association alone does not establish which variable causes the other or what an intervention would do.
lectures.pitfall: Do not turn co-occurrence into a causal conclusion. A plausible common cause is also not proof that there is no effect between the variables.
lectures.takeaway: Keep the observed pattern, a proposed explanation and the effect of an action separate.

source_refs.locator: Section 1.3, Figure 1.2 and Principle 1.1, association and possible causal explanations

lectures.challenge_title: Shared practical investigation: a different everyday claim

lectures.title: Say what changes and what you will observe
lectures.hook: A fictional question asks whether giving a different drug dose would change recovery. Which part is the proposed change, and which part is the result?
lectures.example_label: Synthetic question; no drug benefit or dosing recommendation is asserted. Expert content review pending.

scenario_image.alt_text: A clinician and patient discuss an unlabeled dose card and recovery journal; neither gives a recommended treatment.

worked_steps.title: Identify the change
worked_steps.text: The drug dose is the feature the question proposes changing. In causal reasoning, the word treatment names the intervention of interest.

worked_steps.title: Identify the outcome
worked_steps.text: Recovery is the result the question asks about. Naming it tells us what consequence of the change we want to understand.

worked_steps.title: Write the question
worked_steps.text: What would happen to recovery if the dose were changed? Recognising this question type does not answer whether the change would help.

lectures.definition: A treatment-and-outcome question asks what happens to an outcome when a treatment is changed. Treatment can also mean a non-medical intervention, such as a changed service process.
lectures.pitfall: Naming a treatment and outcome is not evidence that the treatment has a beneficial effect.
lectures.takeaway: Complete the sentence: if we changed this treatment, what would happen to this outcome?
lectures.challenge_title: Fresh case: changing a service process

lectures.title: Recording a choice is different from assigning it
lectures.hook: A fictional clinic records how long patients already sleep. Has recording those values changed anyone's sleep duration?
lectures.example_label: Synthetic teaching example; no sleep intervention or health effect is asserted. Expert content review pending.

scenario_image.alt_text: A person sleeps while a plain wristband passively records sleep; it is not shown assigning a sleep duration.

worked_steps.title: Describe the record
worked_steps.text: The clinic reads durations that already occurred. The act described in this example is recording existing values.

worked_steps.title: Contrast an assignment
worked_steps.text: A different example would deliberately assign a sleep schedule. That would change how the value was set rather than simply read it.

worked_steps.title: Check how the value arose
worked_steps.text: Sorting people by their existing durations is still observation. Ask whether someone deliberately set the value, not just whether two groups were compared.

lectures.definition: Observation records existing values. An intervention deliberately sets or changes a variable, replacing how that value would otherwise be produced.
lectures.pitfall: Selecting cases with a particular value is not the same action as setting that value.
lectures.takeaway: Ask who, if anyone, assigned the value in the situation being described.

source_refs.locator: Section 3.2, page 34, interventions and do notation

lectures.challenge_title: Fresh case: observing people's existing choices

lectures.title: Keep the system, its records and an explanation apart
lectures.hook: A researcher has fictional measurements and a sketch of a hidden disease process. Are the measurements and the sketch the same kind of information?
lectures.example_label: Synthetic records and proposed explanation; not a verified disease mechanism. Expert content review pending.

worked_steps.title: Name the world
worked_steps.text: The world is the system producing the observations. Its processes may be only partly visible to the researcher.

worked_steps.title: Name the data
worked_steps.text: The recorded measurements are data. They show what was observed, rather than every hidden step that produced it.

worked_steps.title: Name the model
worked_steps.text: The sketch is a proposed explanation of how the system might work. It represents the researcher's model rather than another measured record.

lectures.definition: The world is the partly hidden system, data are its observed records, and a model is an explanation of how that system may work.
lectures.pitfall: A well-drawn explanation does not become observed data merely because it looks precise.
lectures.takeaway: Label each piece of information: system, observation or explanatory model.

source_refs.locator: Sections 1.1 and 1.3, pages 2 and 5-6, observations and causal models

lectures.challenge_title: Fresh case: explaining a different hidden system

lectures.title: Distinguish a recorded pattern from a proposed reason
lectures.hook: Fictional museum records show that busier visitor days also have more cafe sales. Is the claim that school holidays cause both patterns recorded directly?
lectures.example_label: Synthetic museum records and hypothetical explanation; no real visitor or sales finding. Expert content review pending.

worked_steps.title: State what the records support
worked_steps.text: The fictional records contain a pattern between visitor counts and cafe sales. Report that observed relationship first.

worked_steps.title: Identify the extra claim
worked_steps.text: Saying school holidays cause both higher visitor counts and more sales adds a proposed causal reason. It is not the same statement as saying the two recorded quantities vary together.

worked_steps.title: Make the assumption visible
worked_steps.text: Write: our proposed explanation assumes that school holidays influence both. The supplied pattern does not directly establish this explanation; stating the assumption separately keeps its status clear.

lectures.definition: Data can support an observed pattern. A causal direction or mechanism adds an assumption about how the pattern is produced.
lectures.pitfall: A familiar or plausible explanation is still different from a direct observation of that explanation.
lectures.takeaway: Use separate sentences for what the records show and what the causal explanation assumes.

source_refs.locator: Sections 1.2-1.4, pages 4-10, causal assumptions and equivalent observations

lectures.challenge_title: Fresh case: data or an additional causal assumption?

lectures.title: Return to the umbrella case as a DAG
lectures.hook: In the umbrella investigation you proposed that rain influences both umbrella carrying and wet pavement. We can now give that picture a formal name: a directed acyclic graph, or DAG.
lectures.example_label: Synthetic proposed diagram; arrows are assumptions, not measured effects. Expert content review pending.

worked_steps.title: Name the three nodes
worked_steps.text: Rain, umbrella carrying and pavement wetness are variables. Each box is a node; a particular rainy arrival is a value or case, not another node.

worked_steps.title: Read the two arrows
worked_steps.text: Rain → umbrella carrying and Rain → pavement wetness represent the simulator's supplied causal assumptions. They are not effect sizes, and the observational table alone did not prove those directions.

worked_steps.title: Trace a path without inventing a cause
worked_steps.text: Umbrella carrying ← Rain → pavement wetness is a path through a common cause. It is not a directed path from umbrellas to wet pavement. The graph is acyclic because following arrow directions never brings you back to the starting node.

worked_graph.label: The umbrella simulator's supplied causal model
worked_graph.note: The earlier intervention left wetness unchanged. The complete two-arrow diagram additionally uses the simulator's supplied assumptions; that one test did not uniquely identify this graph.

lectures.definition: In a DAG, nodes represent variables, arrows represent proposed directions, and paths are connected routes through arrows.
lectures.pitfall: Do not read an arrow as a recorded number or as proof that the proposed direction is true.
lectures.takeaway: Name the graphical feature first: node, arrow or path. Then ask which assumption it represents.
lectures.challenge_title: Fresh case: a route through another proposed diagram

lectures.title: A changed chance is not a guarantee
lectures.hook: A fictional teaching simulator declares that assigning Treatment T increases recovery probability, but some simulated treated cases do not recover. Is that a contradiction?
lectures.example_label: Treatment T and its effects are supplied simulator assumptions, not clinical findings or recommendations. Expert content review pending.

worked_steps.title: Read the supplied assumption
worked_steps.text: The simulator declares a higher recovery probability under assigned Treatment T. This is a given property of the teaching model, not a treatment effect inferred from patient records.

worked_steps.title: Allow different outcomes
worked_steps.text: A higher recovery probability can coexist with some simulated treated cases not recovering. A better chance does not make the favourable outcome certain.

worked_steps.title: Separate probability from certainty
worked_steps.text: The model changes what is likely across cases. It does not say that every individual case must have the same result.

lectures.definition: A cause can change an outcome's probability without determining every individual outcome.
lectures.pitfall: One case with an unfavourable result does not turn a stipulated probability change into a deterministic guarantee.
lectures.takeaway: Ask whether the claim concerns a changed chance or a certain result for every case.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.3, pages 91-92, intervention effects on distributions

lectures.challenge_title: Fresh case: a probabilistic onboarding effect

lectures.title: Separate a clinical variable from its reading
lectures.hook: A fictional clinic records resting heart rates of 64, 72 and 80 beats per minute. Which part names the variable, and which parts are values?
lectures.example_label: Synthetic clinical records; no real patient data. Expert content review pending.

scenario_image.alt_text: A clinician reviews anonymised heart-rate records while patients rest; the picture is context, not the fictional measurements.

worked_steps.title: Name the clinical feature
worked_steps.text: Resting heart rate is the feature collected for each patient. The variable's name tells us what each reading concerns.

worked_steps.title: Read one patient's value
worked_steps.text: A value of 72 beats per minute is one reading of heart rate. It is not a separate variable called 72.

worked_steps.title: Keep the variable across cases
worked_steps.text: Other patients or later records can have different readings. The feature stays resting heart rate even when its value changes.

lectures.definition: A variable can take different values across cases or times. A particular measurement is a value of that variable.
lectures.pitfall: Repeated identical readings in a small dataset do not, by themselves, mean the clinical feature cannot vary.
lectures.takeaway: Name the feature, the case and the reading before comparing patients.
lectures.challenge_title: Fresh clinical case: a hospital dashboard count

lectures.title: Describe what clinical records show
lectures.hook: In fictional clinic records, patients reporting more weekly walking also tend to have lower resting heart rates. What pattern has been recorded?
lectures.example_label: Synthetic clinical example; not a finding about exercise or heart health. Expert content review pending.

scenario_image.alt_text: A clinician discusses a plain clipboard with a patient in a fictional clinic; the illustration does not supply the example records.

worked_steps.title: Identify both measurements
worked_steps.text: The records include reported walking and resting heart rate. Each patient's row contains a value for each variable.

worked_steps.title: Describe their relationship
worked_steps.text: In this supplied dataset, higher walking values tend to occur with lower heart-rate values. Association can run in opposite directions.

worked_steps.title: State the observed pattern
worked_steps.text: Report that relationship across the recorded cases. A single low heart-rate measurement is not itself the relationship between walking and heart rate.

lectures.definition: An observed association is a pattern in how variables occur together or vary together in clinical records.
lectures.pitfall: Do not require both values to increase. A recorded relationship can involve one increasing while the other decreases.
lectures.takeaway: Describe the two variables and the recorded pattern before asking for an explanation.

source_refs.locator: Section 1.1, pages 1-2, joint observations and distributions

lectures.challenge_title: Fresh clinical case: portal use and appointment attendance

lectures.title: A group difference is not yet a treatment effect
lectures.hook: A fictional clinic records poorer recovery among patients receiving Treatment A. Does that recorded difference establish that Treatment A harms recovery?
lectures.example_label: Treatment A and these records are fictional; possible mechanisms are hypotheses. Expert content review pending.

scenario_image.alt_text: A clinician and patients in a fictional clinic provide context without showing a treatment-effect conclusion.

worked_steps.title: Report the group difference
worked_steps.text: Treatment receipt and recovery differ across the fictional recorded groups. This describes an association, not the outcome of assigning different treatments to comparable patients.

worked_steps.title: Consider a possible shared explanation
worked_steps.text: Patients with more severe illness might be more likely to receive Treatment A and less likely to recover. This is a hypothesis about the records, not an established explanation.

worked_steps.title: Keep the treatment question open
worked_steps.text: The group difference alone does not establish harm, benefit or no effect. A possible severity difference does not settle the treatment's effect either.

worked_graph.label: Possible explanation, not established by the clinic records
worked_graph.note: Only proposed common-cause paths are shown. This partial hypothesis does not assert that severity explains everything or that Treatment A has no effect.

lectures.definition: Association describes how variables vary together. A recorded association alone does not establish a causal direction or a treatment effect.
lectures.pitfall: Poorer recovery in a treated group is not, by itself, proof of harm. A plausible alternative explanation is not proof of benefit or no effect.
lectures.takeaway: Separate the observed group difference, a proposed explanation and the effect of assigning treatment.

source_refs.locator: Section 1.3, Figure 1.2 and Principle 1.1, association and possible causal explanations

lectures.challenge_title: Shared neutral investigation: apply the same distinction to a new case

lectures.title: Frame the clinical change and its outcome
lectures.hook: A fictional clinician asks what would happen to recovery if a drug dose were changed. What is being changed, and what result is being asked about?
lectures.example_label: Synthetic question about a fictional treatment; no benefit or dose recommendation. Expert content review pending.

scenario_image.alt_text: A clinician and patient discuss an unlabeled dose card and a recovery journal without any recommended treatment.

worked_steps.title: Specify the treatment
worked_steps.text: The proposed change concerns drug dose. Here treatment names the intervention whose consequence the question asks about.

worked_steps.title: Specify the outcome
worked_steps.text: Recovery is the result of interest. A clear outcome tells the reader which consequence of the proposed change matters.

worked_steps.title: Recognise the question, not an answer
worked_steps.text: What would happen to recovery if the dose changed? This is a treatment-and-outcome question even though no direction or size of effect has been established.

lectures.definition: A treatment-and-outcome question asks what would happen to an outcome if a treatment were changed.
lectures.pitfall: A well-framed clinical question does not prove that the proposed treatment helps or harms.
lectures.takeaway: State the proposed treatment change and name the outcome you want to understand.
lectures.challenge_title: Fresh clinical case: physiotherapy schedule and mobility

lectures.title: Reading a patient record is not assigning a value
lectures.hook: A fictional clinic reads patients' existing sleep durations from their records. Did the clinic assign those durations by recording them?
lectures.example_label: Synthetic records; no real sleep intervention or health effect. Expert content review pending.

scenario_image.alt_text: A person sleeps while a plain wristband passively records sleep; it does not show an assigned sleep duration.

worked_steps.title: Identify the observation
worked_steps.text: The clinic records sleep that already occurred. No assigned sleep duration is described in this example.

worked_steps.title: Imagine a different action
worked_steps.text: A separate fictional study might deliberately assign a schedule. That changes how a value is set instead of merely reading an existing value.

worked_steps.title: Check the assignment process
worked_steps.text: Comparing existing long-sleep and short-sleep groups still records their existing values. Grouping patients does not itself assign their sleep.

lectures.definition: Observation records existing values. An intervention deliberately sets or changes a variable, replacing how that value would otherwise arise.
lectures.pitfall: Selecting patients who already chose an app or behaviour is different from assigning that choice.
lectures.takeaway: Ask how the value arose: was it recorded as it was, or deliberately set?

source_refs.locator: Section 3.2, page 34, interventions and do notation

lectures.challenge_title: Fresh clinical case: patients' existing app choices

lectures.title: Distinguish a patient process from records and a model
lectures.hook: A fictional investigator has laboratory readings and a drawing of how a hidden illness process might produce them. Which object is the explanatory model?
lectures.example_label: Synthetic measurements and hypothetical illness model; no verified disease mechanism. Expert content review pending.

scenario_image.alt_text: A clinician reviews a plain clipboard with a patient in a fictional clinic; it is context, not laboratory evidence.

worked_steps.title: Identify the clinical world
worked_steps.text: The patient's system produces what can be measured. The investigator may not observe every process operating within it.

worked_steps.title: Identify the clinical data
worked_steps.text: The recorded laboratory readings are observations. They are not a complete account of every hidden process.

worked_steps.title: Identify the proposed model
worked_steps.text: The drawing offers an explanation of how the partly hidden system might work. It is a model, rather than another measured laboratory reading.

lectures.definition: The world is the partly hidden system, data are observed records, and a model is an explanation of how that system may work.
lectures.pitfall: Do not treat the labels and arrows in an explanatory drawing as if they were additional measurements.
lectures.takeaway: Keep patient process, observed record and explanatory model distinct.

source_refs.locator: Sections 1.1 and 1.3, pages 2 and 5-6, observations and causal models

lectures.challenge_title: Fresh clinical case: explaining a laboratory device

lectures.title: Mark where a clinical explanation adds an assumption
lectures.hook: Fictional records show that patients who contact a nurse more often also report more symptoms. Is saying illness severity causes both just another description of those records?
lectures.example_label: Synthetic clinical pattern and proposed explanation; not a finding about nursing or illness. Expert content review pending.

scenario_image.alt_text: Patients and a clinician in a fictional clinic provide context without demonstrating why symptoms and clinical contact co-occur.

worked_steps.title: Report the recorded pattern
worked_steps.text: The supplied records contain values for nurse contact and reported symptoms. The fictional example says those variables vary together.

worked_steps.title: Locate the causal explanation
worked_steps.text: Saying severity causes both variables proposes how the pattern might be produced. It adds a mechanism rather than repeating the observed relationship.

worked_steps.title: State its status
worked_steps.text: Write that severity is a proposed shared explanation. It remains an assumption in this example, not a causal mechanism directly established by the records.

lectures.definition: Clinical data can support a pattern. A causal direction or mechanism is an additional assumption that should be stated explicitly.
lectures.pitfall: Clinical plausibility and familiarity do not make a proposed explanation a directly observed fact.
lectures.takeaway: Separate what was recorded from what the clinical causal model assumes.

source_refs.locator: Sections 1.2-1.4, pages 4-10, causal assumptions and equivalent observations

lectures.challenge_title: Fresh clinical case: recorded contact or a proposed cause?

lectures.title: Use the umbrella investigation to read a DAG
lectures.hook: Recall the shared umbrella investigation. Its three-variable picture is a useful starting point for reading clinical diagrams: first name variables, then proposed causal directions.
lectures.example_label: Synthetic proposed clinical diagram; no true drug mechanism or effect is asserted. Expert content review pending.

worked_steps.title: Read the nodes before the story
worked_steps.text: Rain, umbrella carrying and pavement wetness are the three nodes. A clinical diagram uses the same convention: a node could name dose or symptom score, rather than one patient's particular reading.

worked_steps.title: Read arrows as assumptions
worked_steps.text: The two rain arrows express the simulator's supplied model. Likewise, a dose → symptom arrow in a clinical hypothesis states a causal direction; the drawing itself is not a clinical result or an effect size.

worked_steps.title: Distinguish a path from a directed path
worked_steps.text: Umbrella carrying ← Rain → pavement wetness is a connected path through a common cause, not a directed path from carrying umbrellas to wetness. A DAG has arrows but no directed cycle; following arrow directions cannot return to the starting node.

worked_graph.label: A familiar general case, now read as a DAG
worked_graph.note: These are the teaching simulator's assumptions. The unchanged intervention result did not, on its own, prove this unique graph. Clinical graphs require their own justified assumptions.

lectures.definition: Nodes represent variables, arrows represent proposed directions, and paths are connected routes through arrows in a DAG.
lectures.pitfall: An arrow in a clinical hypothesis is not a numerical result or proof that the proposed relation is true.
lectures.takeaway: Identify the node, arrow or path, then say which modelling assumption it displays.
lectures.challenge_title: Fresh clinical case: a path through a different proposed diagram

lectures.title: A treatment probability is not an individual promise
lectures.hook: A fictional teaching simulator declares that assigning Treatment T increases recovery probability, but some simulated treated cases do not recover. Can both statements hold?
lectures.example_label: Treatment T and its effects are supplied simulator assumptions, not clinical findings or recommendations. Expert content review pending.

worked_steps.title: Read the given simulator rule
worked_steps.text: The teaching model stipulates a higher recovery probability under assigned Treatment T. The example does not infer this effect from an observed treated group.

worked_steps.title: Allow variation across cases
worked_steps.text: A higher recovery chance still allows some simulated patients not to recover. A probability increase does not promise recovery for everyone.

worked_steps.title: Recognise the claim's level
worked_steps.text: The supplied causal effect concerns how likely recovery is across cases. It does not determine the result for every individual case.

lectures.definition: A cause can change an outcome's probability without determining every individual outcome.
lectures.pitfall: Do not interpret a stipulated probability increase as either a guaranteed individual result or evidence of a real treatment benefit.
lectures.takeaway: Keep a changed chance separate from an individual guarantee and from an empirical clinical conclusion.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.3, pages 91-92, intervention effects on distributions
